title: New wave of Democratic attorneys general may reshape the justice system
body:
Texas Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson, a Democrat, is seen speaking on the state Senate floor in Austin on Sept. 3, 2025.
                
                    Eric Gay/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Eric Gay/AP
    

   
   The nation's legal landscape is set for a major shift after voters elected Democrats to serve as attorney general in five formerly Republican-led states. That means a majority of states will soon have a Democrat serving as the top law enforcement officer.   Democratic candidates flipped attorneys general offices in Georgia, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio and Texas–and in Alaska, the incoming Democratic governor announced his pick for attorney general in a state previously run by Republicans.   The Democratic victories could have major effects for what alleged crimes are investigated, lawsuits filed and court cases heard across the U.S. State attorneys general typically have sweeping discretion in what legal challenges to bring or drop on behalf of their state's residents.   
   And with roughly seven in ten Americans set to live in a state with a Democratic attorney general, Democrats will be able to bring many more cases across the country that argue for their positions on the economy, environment, abortion, civil rights, and crime, rather than the Republican perspective.   "Voters picked AGs who will stand up and fight for them, whether that's taking on rising costs, pushing back against a lawless administration, or holding bad actors accountable. It's a time to celebrate, and also to get to work," Democratic Attorneys General Association President Sean Rankin said in a statement to NPR.   Conversely, the midterm election defeats for Republicans attorneys general candidates left the conservative legal movement reeling – and planning a comeback.   "There's no sugarcoating it, this was the worst election for Republicans since 1974," said Adam Piper, executive director of the Republican Attorneys General Association.   In an interview with NPR, Piper contended that Republican attorneys generals' policies are still broadly supported by voters, but were overshadowed by the unpopularity of the rest of the GOP. He noted that Republican attorneys general candidates ran ahead of GOP candidates for governor and U.S. Senate in some states.   Following the midterm results, Republican attorneys general convened for their fall meeting in Dallas, Texas, where the outgoing attorney general, Ken Paxton, lost his bid for Senate. He will soon be replaced by a Democrat, Nathan Johnson.   
   Piper said attendees grimly reflected on their challenges while also strategizing how to position Republican attorneys general to support the GOP as 2028 approaches. He added that the Republican Attorneys General Association are watching for potential "lawfare" by Democrats, including changing the number of Supreme Court justices or welcoming new states into the Union.   "We have to have better quality of candidates at the top of the ticket," Piper said. "We have to have better message discipline, and we need other committees in Washington to focus on what RAGA has done, and that is making sure we're good stewards of resources."   Democratic attorneys general held their own conference in Chicago, which some attendees said was both a celebration of the Democratic victories and an orientation for the incoming Democratic attorneys general.   "While a lot of the focus turns to what's next in Washington, we understand and we're not naive to the fact that we will continue to have a critical role in protecting our republic," said Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul during a Nov. 19 press briefing with other Democratic attorneys general.   Johnson, the incoming Texas attorney general, said at the same briefing that the wins for Democrats in the state house and governor's mansion could prompt Republicans to cooperate on a "cleansing" anti-corruption agenda. But he also signaled he'd support legislation and legal challenges to President Donald Trump's efforts to build a wall in Big Bend National Park on Texas' border with Mexico.   The Texas attorney general has traditionally brought cases on behalf conservative legal causes that had wide-ranging impacts across the country. The office also served as a training ground for Republican legal talent. U.S. Sen. John Cornyn and Texas Gov. Greg Abbott both served as attorney general before seeking higher office, while Sen. Ted Cruz served as solicitor general in the office before running for Congress. Other staffers have gone on to serve as judges, law clerks and prosecutors.   
   "Texas was a major intellectual force for the Republican attorneys general, and that's not going to be easily replaced," said James Tierney, a professor at Harvard Law School who has advised more than thirty attorneys general from both parties on staffing and legal philosophy.   "There are a lot of very smart, good lawyers in various AG offices who are very conservative," said Tierney. "But they don't have the heft and the size and the number of attorneys that Texas brings, and so for them, it's a very significant loss."   For Democrats, the recent wins could transform how the states enforce laws, bring legal cases, and support or hinder the Trump administration.   "These new attorneys general are not going to be particularly favorable towards the Trump administration, and will take an oppositional position in a number of different cases," said Anthony Michael Kreis, a constitutional law professor at Georgia State University. That may mean direct lawsuits against the administration in coalition with other attorneys general, Kreis said.   Many incoming Democratic attorneys general campaigned on bringing cases against alleged price gouging and digital surveillance by companies, as well as a tougher approach to antitrust concerns. But they will also face pressure to listen to their local business communities–including major multinational corporations.   "I think it's actually likely to increase bipartisan coalitions, particularly on economic issues," said Swain Wood, a partner at the law firm WilmerHale who now co-chairs the firm's practice advising clients on state attorneys general. Wood, who served as assistant attorney general to North Carolina Democratic Attorney General Josh Stein, cited past landmark settlements against tobacco and opioid distributors as cases where bipartisan groups of attorneys general found common ground.   Attorneys general from both parties have also banded together in recent years on cases about regulating social media platforms. Democrats elected in newly-minted swing states may already face pressure to choose popular or bipartisan legal actions. That's one way to maintain voters' support, as they're likely to face stiff reelection challenges.

title: Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., shares why he opposes Trump's proposed tariffs
description: NPR's A Martinez speaks with Virginia Sen. Tim Kaine about the Democrat's opposition to President Trump's new tariffs.
body:
NPR's A Martinez speaks with Virginia Sen. Tim Kaine about the Democrat's opposition to President Trump's new tariffs.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    A MARTÍNEZ, HOST:  All right. Let's go now to one of the lawmakers who's been trying to fight the president's tariffs in Congress. Democratic Senator Tim Kaine of Virginia backed multiple bills meant to curb or refund the administration's tariffs, including legislation that would constrain the president's ability to impose new tariffs at all.Senator, happy Thanksgiving. Thanks for joining us on Turkey Day.TIM KAINE: A, very glad to be with you. And our Turkey Day is going to cost about 6% more than it cost last year...MARTÍNEZ: (Laughter).KAINE: ...Partly because of tariffs. So this is a good topic.MARTÍNEZ: Well, let's get into that. So the president says the objective is to counter unfair foreign trade practices. What's your view of that rationale?KAINE: Well, in the big picture, what the president has said is this tariff strategy applied everywhere is going to increase manufacturing jobs in the United States. To the contrary, manufacturing jobs in the United States have declined during President Trump's second term. He also said it would reduce our trade deficit. The trade deficit has increased during President Trump's second term. So neither of the goals that he has have been achieved by his tariff strategy. And one of the things he promised to do - bring prices down - has been dramatically affected in the negative way you saw the inflation numbers yesterday. We're seeing dramatic inflation driven by tariffs in the Iran war. So this is an economic strategy that is a big failure.MARTÍNEZ: You mentioned manufacturing jobs are not happening in the way that we were told they would happen. But how do you square that with the Steelworkers Union who says that the new tariffs are long overdue?KAINE: There are particular sectors that like them. I mean, the steel industry likes more steel production in the U.S. But overall, if you look at manufacturing, generally, manufacturing jobs are down. They were up during the Biden administration. They're down during the Trump administration with President Trump saying that the tariffs were going to cause this big manufacturing renaissance.MARTÍNEZ: So I mentioned your efforts in the Senate to fight the president's tariffs. What is your strongest argument for passing legislation to stop the president from imposing these particular tariffs?KAINE: So there's a broad argument, and then there's kind of a narrow focused one. So here's the broad one. The Constitution gives tariff power to Congress, not the president. And Congresses of both parties, in my view, have made mistakes over decades in handing off this power, delegating it to the president and allowing the president to impose tariffs on his own. Just to allow one person to impose taxes is not a good idea. And so there are a variety of strategies. I - we - I did work with Senator Paul of Kentucky, and we led the effort against the president's use of the IEEPA statute to impose tariffs. The Supreme Court ultimately struck down...MARTÍNEZ: International Emergency Economic Powers Act, yeah.KAINE: That's right, yeah. And the Supreme Court ultimately struck down any imposition of tariffs under that statute. But we're looking at the remaining statutes that Congress has sort of handed the power to the president in one of two ways. You can either repeal those statutes and eliminate any presidential ability to impose tariffs. Or recognizing that presidents sometimes need to move quick - quicker than Congress can - you could allow the president to impose tariffs for a limited period of time, say 60 or 90 days, but those tariffs would expire unless Congress affirmatively validates them and continues them.So those are some of the legal solutions that are on the table. And with Democratic majorities, I think we have a very good chance of getting some of these bills to President Trump's desk.MARTÍNEZ: You have 56 U.S. senators in - next year. What's the likelihood that you're going to get enough Republicans that share your view? You mentioned Rand Paul, but you're going to need more if you want to pass legislation that the president can't veto.KAINE: We will. We - my prediction is we're going to get enough Republican votes in the aftermath of the election, which was really a repudiation of tariffs and the war. We'll get enough Republican votes to put tariff bills on President Trump's desk. Now, here comes the next challenge. If he vetoes those bills, would we have enough to have a two-thirds vote in both Houses to override his veto? That's a - more of an uphill climb. But we're going to test that. We're going to put bills on his desk, dramatically limiting his tariff powers to try to help Americans' pocketbooks. And then we'll say to him, if you veto this bill, you're just going to hurt people. So why don't you just sign it?MARTÍNEZ: What message do you think these new tariffs are sending to U.S. trading partners? I mean, it's been a few years of, you know, going back and forth on tariffs.KAINE: Yeah. A, I mentioned there's sort of a narrower argument on tariffs, and now you're asking me about that. Tariffs have a place. And I think most have agreed that China has been really ripping off the United States in trade. You know, theft of intellectual property, state subsidies of industries that then try to undercut American jobs. The strategy up to President Trump had always been, let's link arms with our allies - the EU, Japan, Korea, Canada. And let's all impose consequences on China for being a trade rule violator. The message that's being sent by the Trump administration is, hey, we're decoupling with allies, and we're just going to wage war individually against all of you. That makes the effort against China much less likely to succeed than if we instead linked our arms with our allies, didn't impose tariffs against them, and focused at what I think everybody agrees is the main trade violator in the world, which is China.MARTÍNEZ: Senator, we've got about 30 seconds left. Have you thought about what the next two years are going to be like to try and work together with the president to make Americans' lives more - less expensive?KAINE: I think what the Dems need to do is put a lot of bills on his desk. And we can get Republican help on some, but we also have some mechanisms like budget reconciliation where we can do bills just with Democratic votes. Put good bills on his desk that help everyday people and say, Mr. President, if you want to help folks, you'll sign this. And if you don't sign it, you're going to let people know you don't care about them.MARTÍNEZ: All right. That is Democratic Senator Tim Kaine of Virginia. Once again, happy Thanksgiving and thanks for coming on.KAINE: Thanks, A. Be good.

title: Trump administration proposes new tariffs on goods from major U.S. trading partners
description:
President Trump's new proposed tariffs are already meeting pushback from Democrats and some free trade advocates.   

    
        
          T
body:
President Trump's new proposed tariffs are already meeting pushback from Democrats and some free trade advocates.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    A MARTÍNEZ, HOST:  The Trump administration is proposing new tariffs on goods from 14 of the U.S.'s biggest trading partners, including Japan, the EU and China. It's arguing that these new tariffs fight other countries' unfair trade practices, but it's not clear that they will actually do that.For more, we have NPR White House correspondent Danielle Kurtzleben. Danielle, what did the White House outline yesterday?DANIELLE KURTZLEBEN, BYLINE: Well, it's new proposed tariffs on goods from major trading partners - the ones you mentioned, and also South Korea and Cambodia, for example. And the rates could go as high as 40% on Chinese goods, also 35% on goods from Vietnam and 20 or 25% on goods from other countries. They're also proposing additional tariffs on sugar and aircrafts from Brazil, and that would add to previous tariffs the U.S. imposed there.MARTÍNEZ: When could these plans actually become real?KURTZLEBEN: Well, they could go into effect within a couple of months. That's what U.S. Trade Ambassador Jamieson Greer said yesterday. Now, as for what the rates will be, well, that's still unclear, and that's because for each country, excepting those additional tariffs on Brazil, the White House has two rates they've listed - a proposed rate and a deal rate. To give an example, the tariff on China could be 20%. That's the deal rate. But depending in part on how ongoing discussions go, the rates on Chinese goods could go as high as 40%.MARTÍNEZ: Forty percent. Now, yeah, the Supreme Court struck down some of Trump's earlier tariffs. So how is the White House legally justifying these new ones?KURTZLEBEN: Well, these are being implemented under a law known for short as Section 301, which is meant to counter other countries' unfair trade practices. And so here the White House is alleging that these other countries have what's called structural excess capacity in various manufactured goods. And the administration has described this as when another country has policies that cause a good to be overproduced, which then distorts a global market for that good. And so those practices, according to the administration, can include all sorts of things, like labor practices, subsidies and tax breaks.Now, the administration imposed other sweeping 301 tariffs earlier this year, and there's a lawsuit in process challenging those, with the key argument being that those tariffs were just way broader than the 301 law calls for.MARTÍNEZ: Now, you mentioned a lawsuit. Could these new tariffs face similar legal challenges?KURTZLEBEN: You know, they could. We'll see what happens. But I talked to Sara Albrecht. She's chairman and CEO of the nonpartisan Liberty and Justice Center (ph), which filed that lawsuit against those earlier tariffs. And she said these new tariffs are not being used the way 301 tariffs are supposed to.SARA ALBRECHT: It is a negotiating tactic. That is not what tariffs, in a broad sense, are supposed to be. Like, you can do that on a country-by-country basis if they're addressing a specific problem, not just general, hey, we want better trade deals.KURTZLEBEN: In addition, both she and other trade experts say they think the White House is just proposing these new tariffs as a way to replace the sweeping tariffs the Supreme Court struck down earlier this year.MARTÍNEZ: Now, we all just found out how unpopular these tariffs were in the midterm elections. So how are these new tariffs landing politically?KURTZLEBEN: Well, we've heard some real pushback from congressional Democrats. Richard Neal, top House Democrat on the Ways and Means Committee, said in a statement, quote, "Trump is putting everything from family budgets to our national security at risk to keep his tariff scheme in place."Now, congressional Republicans have been quieter, and this does come a few weeks after they lost dozens of seats in the election, which is widely attributed, in large part, to high prices, and tariffs do cause higher prices.MARTÍNEZ: All right, that's NPR's Danielle Kurtzleben. Danielle, thanks a lot.KURTZLEBEN: Of course.

title: Postmortem of AI ads
description:
The data AI companies have been accumulating in this cycle will help serve future ads to hyper-specific audiences.
    
        
          Transcript
body:
The data AI companies have been accumulating in this cycle will help serve future ads to hyper-specific audiences.
    
        
          Transcript
        
    SCOTT DETROW, HOST:  The midterm election was a big moment for AI political advertising. Campaigns spent at least $187 million on ads, either generated or enhanced by artificial intelligence. That's according to the nonpartisan Wesleyan Media Project. These ads did not appear to affect the overall outcomes of this election, but that's not going to stop campaigns from making more of them in the next cycle. NPR political reporter Maham Javaid has more.MAHAM JAVAID, BYLINE: Many New York voters saw a spot featuring an AI-generated avatar of Governor Kathy Hochul earlier this year. It's a deepfake, where she appears in various settings, like in front of a windmill and a hotel lobby, saying...(SOUNDBITE OF AD)AI-GENERATED VOICE: (As Kathy Hochul) We provided luxury accommodations for illegal migrants in beautiful hotels just like this.JAVAID: The ad, which came with an AI disclaimer, was paid for by Hochul's Republican opponent for the gubernatorial seat, Bruce Blakeman.(SOUNDBITE OF AD)AI-GENERATED VOICE: (As Kathy Hochul) This November, don't let Bruce Blakeman lower your taxes or make New York safe. Keep it unsafe and unaffordable with Kathy Hochul as your governor.JAVAID: Hochul won the race handily by roughly 20 points. More than 90% of the millions of dollars spent on AI ads were supporting Republican candidates, many of whom lost. The ads often did not connect with voters, says Basil Smikle, a Democratic strategist. But he says campaigns will keep using them.BASIL SMIKLE: You could create an ad that has a lot more shock value than a typical live-action video and produce them more quickly.JAVAID: They're also much cheaper, says GOP strategist Brian Ruddle.BRIAN RUDDLE: If you're a candidate who does not have a big budget, can't go out and hire a television production company, but you've got a good message and something that can break through.JAVAID: That's where AI can help, Ruddle says. And as the technology gets better, it'll get harder to detect what is real.RUDDLE: It is not just about convincing some people that fake things are real. Sometimes it's about people thinking that real things are now fake.JAVAID: Jason Riley is a retired Navy pilot from Austin, Texas. He says this time around, the AI ads he saw didn't fool him or sway his vote. But about 61% of Americans are concerned that audio or video deepfakes did affect the election's outcome. That's according to the UC San Diego Center for Transparent and Trusted Elections. Some voters are concerned about the technology's ability to misguide them, including Steve Geller (ph), a book editor from Sacramento, California.STEVE GELLER: I think it's not worth having a society which allows this, even though I do think it can be effective for a politician to use it.JAVAID: This cycle, AI collected a lot of voter data, which could be useful to campaigns, says Brendan Steinhauser, another GOP strategist.BRENDAN STEINHAUSER: AI-generated ads that are running to specific individuals based on their behavior online.JAVAID: That means, he says, very targeted ads at scale that are going to be more effective over time.Maham Javaid, NPR News.(SOUNDBITE OF TOMMY GUERRERO'S "BY THE SEA AT THE END OF THE WORLD")

title: Court lets Puerto Rico governor fire firm that runs the island's troubled power grid
description: Puerto Rico Supreme Court allows governor to fire company that runs the island's troubled power grid
body:
Puerto Rico Supreme Court allows governor to fire company that runs the island's troubled power grid
    
            
                
                Transcript
            
        
                Download
                
                
                    
                        
                            
                            Embed
                        
                        
                            <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6054139/nx-s1-10020784" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
                        
                    
                
                
                  
                    
                    Transcript
                  
                
        
    



      LUMA Energy took over the electric grid five years ago. The court's ruling nullifies its contract, and gives the government a year to find a new operator.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    A MARTÍNEZ, HOST:  Puerto Rico's supreme court has ruled the island's governor can kick out the private company that's been running its troubled power grid for five years. The decision could have huge consequences for electric service in Puerto Rico. Here is NPR's Adrian Florido.ADRIAN FLORIDO, BYLINE: After Hurricane Maria flattened Puerto Rico's already rickety power grid in 2017, the island's government privatized it. It gave a company called LUMA Energy, based in Canada and Texas, a 15-year deal to take over the power lines, promising that LUMA would rebuild the grid stronger and improve the notoriously unreliable service. LUMA took over in 2021. But things have not gone as planned.Blackouts are still a constant fact of life. LUMA has come in for harsh criticism from customers and officials. Last year, Governor Jenniffer Gonzalez-Colon filed suit to nullify LUMA's contract. Yesterday, the Puerto Rican Supreme Court ruled in her favor that LUMA must go.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)JENNIFFER GONZALEZ-COLON: Today is a day of celebration on the island.FLORIDO: This is the governor speaking after the ruling. She said LUMA has not lived up to its promises.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)GONZALEZ-COLON: More outages on the island, more shutdowns on the island. They have not fulfilled the requirements of the contract.FLORIDO: In fact, the island's supreme court ruled on procedural grounds, saying officials had not followed local requirements when approving agreements with the company. The court gave the local government a year to put a new operator in place. The governor said the work to find a new private company will start immediately.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)GONZALEZ-COLON: It's going to be a good transition. We're going to make it in a year. And I hope that all companies that are interested in participating in this process will fulfill and follow the process of law. And we're going to be opening that process for public bid.FLORIDO: The court gave LUMA Energy 10 days to request a reconsideration of its ruling. In a statement, LUMA said it is considering its legal options. The company has long argued that the grid it took over was in awful shape and that it is not fully to blame for the blackouts. A new operator will need approval from both the local government and a federal oversight board that Congress put in place 10 years ago to get Puerto Rico out of bankruptcy. In a statement, that board criticized the governor for ending LUMA' s contract without having a new company ready to go. It said it's worried about the continuity of service on the island. In her remarks yesterday, the governor said she has a plan in place and will reveal it soon.Adrian Florido, NPR News.(SOUNDBITE OF TOBACCO'S "BACKWOODS ALTAR")

title: With Abbott out, what does the future look like for data centers in Texas?
description:
With Abbott out, what does the future look like for data centers in Texas?
    
            
                
                Transcript
body:
With Abbott out, what does the future look like for data centers in Texas?
    
            
                
                Transcript
            
        
                Download
                
                
                    
                        
                            
                            Embed
                        
                        
                            <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6048749/nx-s1-10022025" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
                        
                    
                
                
                  
                    
                    Transcript
                  
                
        
    



      Texas has been one of the most welcoming states for data centers, but that might change with a new governor coming in.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    SCOTT DETROW, HOST:  Under Republican Governor Greg Abbott, Texas has been one of the country's most welcoming states for new data centers. Times have changed. Abbott lost his bid for reelection, and Democratic Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has other ideas about data centers. Leigh Walden of member station KUT in Austin reports.LEIGH WALDEN, BYLINE: Kate Goodrich is a lobbyist for the tech industry at K&L Gates, a law firm in Austin. And in the days after the election, people in her business were absorbing the change like everyone else.KATE GOODRICH: The majority of everyone that we're talking to on both sides of the aisle have their mouths somewhere between 1 and 3 inches open still.WALDEN: Their clients range from individual data center developers to some of the multibillion-dollar companies that operate them, like Microsoft. In November of last year, Texas Governor Greg Abbott declared the state the epicenter of AI development. He has signed laws that made large data centers exempt from sales taxes for the equipment they buy. But then this summer, as he campaigned for a fourth term, he changed his tune and said it was time for Texas to start...(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)GREG ABBOTT: ...Pushing back against these AI data centers that are trying to build in our neighborhoods.WALDEN: As the public backlash to data centers grew, he also imposed a pause on all new data center projects while the state studied their impact. That pause has already expired. Meanwhile, Democrat Gina Hinojosa said this on CNN right after her surprising victory for governor.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)GINA HINOJOSA: Right now, what has happened is data centers have moved into mostly rural communities, and there are no rules and laws to protect Texans, and Texans are being taken advantage of.WALDEN: Now people are watching for what she's going to do as the issue plays out across the country after the midterms. Incoming governors in Kansas and Georgia also promise to pause data centers. But because of the size of its economy, Texas often sets a precedent for how other states do business too. John Hall is the CEO and president of Houston Advanced Research Center, which focuses on environmental policy. He expects Hinojosa to impose a moratorium and then new regulations.JOHN HALL: Establish it in policy that data centers should have to bring their own water and bring their own power. But in addition to that, offset their emissions.WALDEN: Austin McCarty, a tech lobbyist at K&L Gates, said some of his clients are okay with more regulation. They think it might build trust and actually improve the industry's reputation.AUSTIN MCCARTY: It's being dragged down by some folks that are not as prepared as the good actors who have really put in a lot of work to show that they're here to be a part of a really important ecosystem here in Texas.WALDEN: Some Texans, though skeptical, seem willing to let the industry work on what they see as making amends. Torrie Martin is a horse rancher outside of San Marcos in Central Texas. She's gone to numerous local government meetings to speak against a proposed data center site near her ranch.TORRIE MARTIN: I am optimistic, but, you know, we have to hold people accountable and pay attention to what is happening.WALDEN: She thinks it's because of the unpopularity of data centers that laws will be passed and bipartisan agreements reached.MARTIN: People on either side or all sides are fighting the same fight, which makes me feel more confident in my decision to, you know, stand up so loudly for the ranch lands and agricultural side to Texas.WALDEN: New state lawmakers will be sworn in January, and then they'll begin a legislative session where data centers will be on the agenda.From NPR News, I'm Leigh Walden in Austin.

title: After Democrats' midterm wins, some hope attacks on DEI will ease
description: After the midterms, a Democratic congressman declared that DEI is back. What does Democrats' ascendance portend for diversity initiatives that
body:
After the midterms, a Democratic congressman declared that DEI is back. What does Democrats' ascendance portend for diversity initiatives that the Trump administration relentlessly attacked?   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    JUANA SUMMERS, HOST:  Since President Trump returned to office, he and his Republican allies have moved aggressively to eliminate diversity, equity and inclusion programs across government and the private sector. After Democrats won resoundingly in this month's midterms, California Democratic Congressman Ro Khanna posted this video.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)RO KHANNA: Tonight, DEI is back as America celebrated diversity and inclusion.SUMMERS: So what could the midterms be signaling about the future of DEI? NPR's Adrian Florido reports.ADRIAN FLORIDO, BYLINE: As a consultant, Lily Zheng helps companies develop programs to improve workplace diversity. Since last year, Zheng has watched most companies retreat from the work, in some cases to do it more quietly and others ending it altogether.LILY ZHENG: It was fear of retribution. It was fear of political and regulatory pressure.FLORIDO: But since Democrats prevailed in the midterms, Zheng says there's been a noticeable vibe shift.ZHENG: Some of my colleagues who have been doing this work with a lower profile have expressed relief, maybe, that now they don't have to be tiptoeing on eggshells, likely.FLORIDO: It's based on a sense, Zheng says - maybe just a hope - that newly empowered Democrats will find ways to rein in Republican attacks that have had a chilling effect on DEI work.ANTONIO INGRAM: I think, with this new political landscape, that chilling effect is thawing out.FLORIDO: Antonio Ingram is an attorney with the NAACP Legal Defense Fund. He says the president's Republican allies in Congress have helped foster a culture of fear around DEI, summoning the leaders of universities, companies and nonprofits to hostile hearings.INGRAM: To cross-examine them and to intimidate them from continuing to do the work they're doing to create a multiracial democracy. And now we have people who are going to be pro-civil rights in control of those committee hearings.FLORIDO: But DEI experts that NPR spoke with said institutions are unlikely to quickly jump right back into diversity work, much less promote it publicly. Shaun Harper runs the Race and Equity Center at the University of Southern California. He's hopeful organizations will find their way back to DEI work. But after watching so many retreat from it so quickly, he says...SHAUN HARPER: I don't expect them to overnight flip on a switch and, you know, declare that DEI is back.FLORIDO: One reason is that President Trump still controls the federal agencies that have used threats of funding cuts and lawsuits to try to force institutions to end DEI programs. In a statement to NPR, White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster called DEI policies, quote, "racist and destructive." The White House accused President Biden of letting them run rampant and said Trump was elected with a mandate to end these policies. Still, in states that have followed the president's lead on DEI, it seems clear that the midterm Democratic wins could usher in a significant shift, like in Texas.LILIANA GARCES: That pressure to remove certain readings from your classroom or self-censor is just not going to be as strong.FLORIDO: Liliana Garces is professor of education at the University of Texas at Austin. She's been studying the impact of state restrictions on DEI programs and race-based curricula. After Republican leaders in Texas banned diversity programs at public universities, she interviewed administrators implementing the bans on their college campuses. And she found that because of the political climate, many feared being accused of not complying.GARCES: There was a lot of uncertainty about the consequences, which meant that administrators were applying the law in very restrictive ways and prohibiting programs that weren't even covered by the law.FLORIDO: Texans this month elected a Democratic governor, a Democratic attorney general and a Democratic majority in the State House of Representatives. Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has said she will not engage in culture wars. Adrian Florido, NPR News.(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)

title: Trump effectively ended asylum. Advocates look to the Supreme Court to restore it
description: A view of the border wall at the U.S.-Me
body:
A view of the border wall at the U.S.-Mexico border near Somerton, Ariz., on Oct. 18.
                
                    Olivier Touron/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Olivier Touron/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   For nearly two years, the Trump administration has prohibited asylum claims at the U.S.-Mexico border, canceled thousands of pending asylum applications and overhauled the immigration court system with mass firings. Critics say that combined, these moves have effectively shut down a once vital pathway for those fleeing persecution or danger.   The U.S. Supreme Court will soon consider whether the president can circumvent Congress and existing federal immigration law and unilaterally suspend access to asylum protections.   The legal challenge to the president's ban, which went into effect within hours of President Trump retaking office, is the latest legal case against the administration's seismic immigration policy changes that will be taken up by the high court. Those policy changes, critics say, have robbed asylum seekers of basic due process rights and have transformed the immigration court system into a deportation arm of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).   
   In legal filings, the Trump administration has insisted the proclamation is a necessary protection against "invasion" along the southern border and what the president and conservative critics have long said is abuse of the system by "fake" asylum seekers. Since it has been in place, the chaotic crush of people crossing into the U.S. has plummeted. U.S. Border Patrol apprehensions dropped to their lowest level in agency history this year. The agency recorded fewer than 99,000 Southwest border apprehensions in fiscal year 2026 — a 95% decline compared with more than 1.8 million per year under President Biden, according to U.S. Customs and Border Protection data.   "The difference between an average month under Trump and an average month under Biden is just staggering," Simon Hankinson, a senior research fellow with the Border Security and Immigration Center at the Heritage Foundation, a conservative think tank closely aligned with Trump, told NPR. And should the Supreme Court reverse the ban, "it would be disastrous," he added.   Hankinson contends that most people arriving at the southern border don't qualify for asylum. "And even if they did, they've already passed through Mexico, which is a safe third country where they could claim asylum, especially if they're coming from Venezuela or Afghanistan. So you have a population that overwhelmingly will not qualify under U.S. law for asylum. They're here because they want to get a job," he said.   
   But, critics say, taken together the administration's moves have gutted access to asylum.   Despite newly restored quiet along the southern border, the president's argument for the asylum ban has been rejected by two lower federal courts. It has, however, remained largely in place as the case is tied up in court battles.   In December, the Supreme Court will review the administration's strategy of deporting immigrants to third countries that have agreed to adjudicate asylum claims, even as some of those countries face human rights abuse allegations and cannot guarantee that the person seeking asylum won't be returned to their home nation.   The administration faces a third legal battle that could end its attempt to indefinitely detain thousands of people in deportation proceedings.   If the majority-conservative court rules in favor of immigrant advocates in the lawsuits, advocates say, the decisions could finally break the choke hold that the Trump administration has had on asylum approvals, which are at their lowest in decades. National asylum denial rates soared to 94% in June, up from about 50% in 2024 — the last full year of the Biden administration. That's according to TRAC, a research project at Syracuse University that tracks data about immigration judges.   "The president does not have the right to unilaterally override the protections Congress has afforded those fleeing danger," said Lee Gelernt, lead counsel and deputy director of the Immigrants' Rights Project at the American Civil Liberties Union, one of the groups behind the challenge to the asylum ban. "The courts are right to reject this unprecedented power grab that would put countless lives in danger. We look forward to making our case before the Supreme Court."   Lawyers for migrants seeking asylum are hoping for wins at the high court. For several of Madhavi Narayanan's clients, this could be lifesaving. A Los Angeles-based immigration attorney with Human Rights First, she is currently representing immigrants who, prior to Trump's second term, would have had what she calls "slam dunk" asylum petitions.   
   One of them is a 30-something Ethiopian man called ZG, who arrived in the U.S. through Mexico in February 2025 after enduring extensive torture in his native country. Narayanan requested that NPR use only ZG because he fears retribution from the Ethiopian government. Upon turning himself in at the southern border, ZG was placed into detention and immediately filed an asylum petition.   Narayanan said ZG is a member of an Indigenous group in Ethiopia that's part of an ongoing armed conflict in that nation, which human rights organizations report is at risk of committing more atrocities against civilians. And, Narayanan, who has been working on the case for nine months, said she has produced documents and letters to support his claims of torture.   "Any other time, it would have been a really straightforward case," she said, adding that "there's a wide, wide range of human rights reports explaining that folks in this exact position would be at high risk" of violence and death if they were to return to Ethiopia.   But instead of an immigration hearing, ZG was given a deportation order this month to Uganda, a country he has never set foot in and one that does not recognize the military violence in Ethiopia as a war.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                An undocumented immigrant prepares to be deported on an Immigration and Customs Enforcement deportation flight bound for El Salvador on Dec. 8, 2010.
                
                    John Moore/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        John Moore/Getty Images
    

   
   In an effort to curb asylum applications and alleviate a crushing backlog of cases for U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, the Trump administration is urging ICE attorneys to terminate asylum claims by convincing immigration judges that an application is incomplete or that a person can't substantiate their claims. Or the administration could argue what it did in ZG's case: that he could apply for asylum in a third country.   It has proved to be a highly successful strategy for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which has so far canceled thousands of pending cases.   
   Narayanan said experiences like ZG's reflect how Trump's changes to immigration courts have all but eliminated due process rights, including evidentiary hearings, clearing the way for summary removals. They also show how new guidelines are designed to limit a judge's autonomy. Recounting the events of the motion to end ZG's claim, Narayanan said the immigration judge told the court that his hands were tied.   "He was basically like, 'OK, I hear everything that you said, but I read this case and I'm not allowed to consider this,'" Narayanan recalled.   According to the Executive Office for Immigration Review, nearly 60 policy memorandums have been issued so far during the second Trump administration — a sharp increase when compared with the 30 immigration-court-related memorandums issued during Biden's four-year term.   The administration has also been aggressive in its pursuit to remake the immigration court bench, purging more than a hundred experienced immigration judges. Jennifer Peyton, a former assistant chief immigration judge in Chicago, told NPR that immigration courts across the country have become unrecognizable.   "Everything is different now," said Peyton, who was fired via email in July 2025 after more than nine years on the bench.   During Trump's first year back in office, nearly 40% of immigration judges were fired or resigned. Nearly all of them have been replaced with what the administration calls "deportation judges," who critics say are ideologically aligned with the president's immigration agenda and keen to rubber-stamp asylum denials and expedited removal orders. That shift, plus Trump's previous appointees, has overhauled the immigration bench. Now more than half of immigration judges are Trump appointees.   Of those new immigration judges, very few have experience working on behalf of migrants. About two-thirds of them come from a homeland security or military legal background, according to an essay in The Yale Law Journal by Geoffrey Heeren, an immigration law and policy professor at the University of Idaho. He wrote that "only about eleven of the new [immigration judges] have clear prior immigrant-defense experience, and of those, only one does not also have DHS or military legal experience."   
   In her previous role, Peyton was part of the immigration-judge hiring-and-training team with the Justice Department. She now practices immigration law representing asylum seekers and appears before the same judges she helped train. In those instances, Peyton said, she feels a bit more at ease because she knows the quality of the training they received. But when she argues cases in front of unfamiliar hires, she said, she's often dismayed.   "There is no doubt in my mind, when I have the misfortune to appear before them, that they don't know the immigration law so much and they don't care that they lack the training that we so rigorously put them through when I was on that team," Peyton said.   She added: "The vast majority have not been taught the process of evaluating a case, but rather the shortcuts to make sure that these procedural roadblocks come up, to make sure that the noncitizens are stripped of their due process."

Storm Postpones Thanksgiving Day Parade, Trump's New Tariffs, Iowa Post-Detonation

                    Transcript
                  
                
        
    



      Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.   Today's top stories   Severe storms sweeping across the nation threaten to cause widespread travel delays today, as millions of people gather with their loved ones. New York City officials announced that the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been rescheduled to Saturday due to the threat of powerful wind gusts that could reach up to 60 mph. This year marked the 100th procession, and the first time the iconic event is being postponed.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Workers inflate the Spider-Man balloon during Macy's Balloon Inflation 2026 on November 25, 2026 in New York City. Macy's plans to celebrate its 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade with a record 100 inflatables, but forecasted high winds are threatening to ground the giant balloons.
                
                    Adam Gray/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Adam Gray/Getty Images
    

   
   🎧 Something is happening across almost every part of the country right now, NPR's Kat Lonsdorf tells Up First. Extreme high tides are affecting the West Coast, snow is expected in parts of the Midwest, and in the South and Southeast, a major storm is advancing up the East Coast. Meteorologist Richard Bann with the National Weather Service Weather Prediction Center tells Lonsdorf the East Coast storm is the primary concern. Bann says the storm will become better organized throughout the day, bringing strong winds and heavy rain that could lead to coastal flooding. The good news: Forecasters expect the East Coast's major storm to move on, mostly wrapping up by Saturday, Lonsdorf says.   
   The Trump administration has proposed new tariffs targeting goods from 14 major U.S. trading partners, including China, Japan and the European Union. Administration officials argue the measures counter unfair foreign trade practices, though critics question their ultimate effectiveness. Proposed rates may reach 40% on Chinese imports, 35% on Vietnamese goods, and 20-25% on products from other targeted nations. Additional tariffs on Brazilian sugar and aircraft are also being suggested.   🎧 U.S. Trade Ambassador Jamieson Greer said that new tariffs could take effect within a couple of months. For each country, the White House has listed a "proposed" rate and a "deal" rate, NPR's Danielle Kurtzleben says. For example, if talks with China progress positively, they may receive a deal rate of 20%, which is different from its proposed rate of 40%. Although the Supreme Court overturned President Trump's previous tariffs, the new ones fall under Section 301, a law meant to counter unfair trade practices. The administration says these countries exhibit "structural excess capacity" in various manufactured goods, a situation caused by policies that lead to overproduction, which can distort the global market.   Federal scientists are testing the air, soil and water in Eastern Iowa for lead contamination after the U.S. Army detonated thousands of pounds of unstable lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown yesterday. Officials said the controlled explosion was the only safe way to dispose of the bomb-making compound.   
   🎧 Eliza Billingham of NPR network station Iowa Public Radio says the major concern is the potential release of lead into the air from the explosion. She adds that the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency has tested the area since the detonation and hasn't found lead in the air. The EPA has deployed around 300 people to sample the air, ground and nearby water. Lead is a neurotoxin that especially endangers children and pregnant people because it can impede childhood development. After a week and a half of delays and inconsistent communication from the Army, residents have grown hesitant about the Army and the EPA's initial findings, Billingham says. Residents want independent monitoring and the University of Iowa and the University of Illinois are conducting regional sampling. Results are expected in a few days and should show if their measurements align with the EPA's data, Billingham says.   A federal judge has blocked Trump from challenging the ABC television network's broadcast licenses. U.S. District Court Judge Loren AliKhan ruled that the president retaliating against satire and commentary he dislikes is unconstitutional. AliKhan issued the preliminary injunction yesterday and dismissed the administration's request to throw out ABC and Disney's lawsuit challenging the review of the local license. Licenses typically last eight years and are rarely revoked. AliKhan's decision drew heavily on Trump's public statements and social media posts against ABC and Disney, as well as comments from Brendan Carr, the president's pick for chair of the Federal Communications Commission.   Life advice   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Our brains are wired to seek out newness, and the retail industry is set up to keep us coming back for more as quickly as possible.
                
                    J Studios/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        J Studios/Getty Images
    

   
   Holiday shopping season is in full swing. Before you spend, consider if you actually need what's in your cart. Sales are exciting because our brains are wired to seek newness. Retailers capitalize on that urge. To escape the cycle of constantly wanting more, shop intentionally and appreciate what you already own, says Eric Athas, author of Saying No to New. He shares his insights on breaking this cycle and finding joy in your current possessions with Life Kit.   
   🛒 Delete the app or remove your credit card info if you have one-click checkout with a company.🛒 Add an item to your online shopping cart and leave it for 24 hours. Research shows that delaying a purchase decreases your interest in it.🛒 Make intentional choices. Don't reject all new things. After you understand this, you can learn to say no to the wrong items and yes to the right ones.🛒 Revisiting old things can provide you with untapped enjoyment in them, research has found. You can apply this by rereading a book or by traveling to a city you have visited before.   For more guidance on how to reclaim joy without seeking newness, listen to this episode of NPR's Life Kit. Subscribe to the Life Kit newsletter for expert advice on love, money, relationships and more.   Picture show   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        Andrea Starr
    

   
   Apple farmers across the Pacific Northwest are ripping out thousands of acres of orchards and grinding trees into mulch because growing the fruit no longer pays. Many say they're being crushed by soaring labor and equipment costs and international tariffs. Even multigenerational growers are leaving land unused rather than hemorrhaging money. Thousands of acres of fruit have been left to rot unpicked on branches, pushing some well-established farms into bankruptcy. Federal farm relief has also largely failed to reach specialty-crop growers. Take a look at photos and videos of affected farms, and read more about how the region that supplies the majority of the U.S.' fresh apples is handling the challenge.   3 things to know before you go   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Aaron Rodgers #8 of the Pittsburgh Steelers walks off the field after their 19-16 loss to the Philadelphia Eagles at Lincoln Financial Field on Nov. 22, 2026, in Philadelphia.
                
                    Emilee Chinn/Getty Images
                
                hide caption

   The Pittsburgh Steelers have cut quarterback Aaron Rodgers after he claimed in an interview that the team's head coach sleeps in meetings.The Ariston Cafe opened in 1924 along Illinois's Route 66, serving classic American diner fare. The National Register landmark attracts international travelers and hosts local milestones, from wedding proposals to 65th anniversaries.In this week's Far-Flung Postcards, NPR's Emily Feng brings readers views of the peak of Mount Kilimanjaro. She was able to see it during a camping trip at altitude.   
   This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.
